item.title: SQL Tutorials : From Basics to Advanced Concepts 2024
item.description:
SQL, or Structured Query Language, serves as the backbone for managing data in databases across various systems like MySQL, SQL Server, MS Access, Oracle, Sybase, Informix, Postgres, and more. In this tutorial, we’ll delve into the fundamental aspects of SQL, exploring its syntax, key commands, and the role it plays in relational database management.

item.title: 5 Types of SQL Database Commands Every Developer Should Know
item.description:
Understanding and mastering SQL database commands is crucial for developers working with relational databases. This article explores five fundamental types of SQL commands that every developer should be familiar with. These commands cover various aspects of database management, including data retrieval, manipulation, and schema management.

1. SELECT - Retrieving Data:

The SELECT statement is fundamental for retrieving data from one or more tables. It allows developers to specify the columns they want to retrieve, apply filtering conditions, and sort the results.

item.title: SQL Tutorial - SQL BETWEEN Operator
item.description:
SQL - BETWEEN Operator

The BETWEEN operator is used to select values within a given range. These values can be numeric, text, or dates.

The BETWEEN operator includes both the start and end values in the range.

BETWEEN Syntax

SELECT column_name(s)
FROM table_name
WHERE column_name BETWEEN value1 AND value2;

Demo Database

BETWEEN Example

The following SQL statement selects all products with prices between 10 and 20.

SELECT * FROM Products
WHERE Price BETWEEN 10 AND 20;

item.title: Tutorial SQL Functions: COUNT(), AVG(), SUM()
item.description:
SQL - COUNT(), AVG(), SUM() Functions

The SQL COUNT(), AVG(), and SUM() functions are powerful tools for retrieving statistical information from a database.

COUNT() Function

The COUNT() function returns the number of rows that match a specified criterion.

COUNT() Syntax

SELECT COUNT(column_name)
FROM table_name
WHERE condition;

COUNT() Example

Consider the following SQL query, which counts the number of products:

SELECT COUNT(ProductID)
FROM Products;

This query returns the total count of products in the database.

item.title: Full SQL Tutorial - Beginners
item.description:
Start Point of SQL

SQL Syntax

SELECT Statement

The SELECT statement is used when retrieving data selectively from a database. The selected data is usually returned in a table format, commonly referred to as a result set. The basic syntax for the SELECT statement is as follows:

SELECT <field_name> FROM <table_name>

Using * retrieves data from all fields, or you can specify field names to fetch data from specific fields.

SELECT * FROM Customers
SELECT CustomerID, Country FROM Customers

In many cases, data fields contain duplicate values. You can use the SELECT DISTINCT statement to retrieve rows with unique values, eliminating duplicates.

item.title: Learn SQL Select: with Examples
item.description:
SQL - SELECT

The SELECT statement is used to retrieve data from a database. The returned data is stored in a table-like structure called a result set.

SELECT Syntax

SELECT column1, column2, ...
FROM table_name;

Here, column1, column2, … are the field names of the table from which you want to select data. To select all available fields in a table, you can use the following syntax:

SELECT * FROM table_name;

item.description:
SQL - DELETE Statement

The DELETE statement is utilized to remove existing records from a table.

DELETE Syntax

DELETE FROM table_name

Note: Exercise caution when deleting records from a table! Be sure to review the WHERE clause of the DELETE statement. The WHERE clause specifies which records will be deleted. Omitting the WHERE clause will result in the deletion of all records from the table!

item.title: SQL ANY and ALL Operators - with Examples
item.description:
SQL ANY and ALL Operators

The SQL ANY and ALL operators are commonly used with the WHERE or HAVING clauses in SQL queries.

ANY Operator

The ANY operator returns True if any of the values in the subquery satisfy the specified condition. The syntax for the ANY operator is as follows:

SELECT column_name(s)
FROM table_name
WHERE column_name operator ANY
(SELECT column_name FROM table_name WHERE condition);

Note: The operator must be a standard comparison operator (=, <>, !=, >, >=, <, or <=).

item.title: SQL HAVING Clause: Examples and Syntax
item.description:
SQL - HAVING

In SQL, the HAVING clause is introduced to complement the WHERE keyword when working with aggregate functions.

HAVING Syntax

SELECT column_name(s)
FROM table_name
WHERE condition
GROUP BY column_name(s)
HAVING condition
ORDER BY column_name(s);

Demo Database

SQL HAVING Examples

Consider the following SQL query, which lists the number of customers in each country, including only countries with more than 5 customers:

SELECT COUNT(CustomerID), Country
FROM Customers
GROUP BY Country
HAVING COUNT(CustomerID) > 5;

item.title: SQL LIKE Operator: For Pattern-Based Search in Database
item.description:
Mastering SQL LIKE Operator: Unleashing Pattern-Based Search

The SQL LIKE operator, a powerful tool in the WHERE clause, enables the search for specified patterns within a column. With two wildcard characters, % and _, this operator opens up a realm of possibilities in pattern-matching.

Understanding the Wildcards

  • %: Represents zero, one, or multiple characters.
  • _: Represents a single character.

Combine % and _ for even more flexible queries!

LIKE Operator Syntax

SELECT column1, column2, ...
FROM table_name
WHERE columnN LIKE pattern;

Multiple conditions can be combined using the AND or OR operators.

item.title: SQL ORDER BY Keyword - With Examples
item.description:
SQL - ORDER BY Keyword

The ORDER BY keyword is employed to sort the result set in ascending or descending order.

  • By default, the ORDER BY keyword arranges records in ascending order.

  • To sort records in descending order, use the DESC keyword.

ORDER BY Syntax

SELECT column1, column2, ...
FROM table_name
ORDER BY column1, column2, ... ASC|DESC;

ORDER BY Example

SELECT * FROM Customers
ORDER BY Country;

ORDER BY DESC Example

Appending DESC at the end sorts the data in descending order.

item.title: SQL Queries: Learn TOP, LIMIT, and ROWNUM in SQL
item.description:
SQL - TOP, LIMIT, ROWNUM

In SQL, the SELECT TOP clause is used to specify the number of records to return.

The SELECT TOP clause proves useful when dealing with large tables that contain thousands of records. Returning a large number of records can impact performance.

Note: It’s important to be aware that not all database systems support the SELECT TOP clause. For instance, MySQL uses the LIMIT clause to select a limited number of records, while Oracle employs ROWNUM.

item.title: SQL SELECT INTO Statement - With Examples
item.description:
SQL SELECT INTO Statement

The SQL SELECT INTO statement is employed to copy data from one table into a new table.

SQL SELECT INTO Syntax

Copy all columns into a new table:

SELECT *
INTO newtable [IN externaldb]
FROM oldtable
WHERE condition;

Copy specific columns into a new table:

SELECT column1, column2, column3, ...
INTO newtable [IN externaldb]
FROM oldtable
WHERE condition;

The new table is created with column names and types as defined in the original table. You can use the AS clause to create new column names.

item.title: SQL UPDATE Statement - With Examples
item.description:
Learn SQL: Usage of the UPDATE Statement

The UPDATE statement in SQL allows for the modification of existing records within a table, offering a powerful tool for data manipulation.

Key Concepts

UPDATE Syntax

UPDATE table_name
SET column1 = value1, column2 = value2, ...
WHERE condition;

Note: Exercise caution when using the UPDATE statement to avoid unintended updates. Always include a WHERE clause to specify the records to be updated. Omitting the WHERE clause will result in updating all records in the table.

item.title: SQL Wildcards - Learn SQL Database Queries
item.description:
## SQL - Wildcard Characters: Boosting Database Query Flexibility

In the realm of SQL, wildcard characters play a crucial role in enhancing the flexibility of queries. These characters are commonly employed in conjunction with the SQL LIKE operator, a powerful tool for searching specific patterns within a column in the WHERE clause. Let's delve into the nuances of these wildcard characters and explore tips to leverage them effectively.

## Understanding Wildcard Characters

In SQL, two primary wildcard characters are frequently utilized:

- `%`: The percent sign signifies zero, one, or multiple characters.
- `_`: The underscore denotes a single character.

It's worth noting that in MS Access and SQL Server, additional wildcard characters like `[charlist]` and `[^charlist]` can be employed to define sets of characters or exclude specific characters.

## Utilizing % and _ Wildcards

Let's explore various LIKE operators with % and _ wildcards:

- **WHERE CustomerName LIKE `a%`**: Finds values starting with 'a'.
- **WHERE CustomerName LIKE `%a`**: Finds values ending with 'a'.
- **WHERE CustomerName LIKE `%or%`**: Locates values with 'or' at any position.
- **WHERE CustomerName LIKE `_r%`**: Identifies values with 'r' in the second position.
- **WHERE CustomerName LIKE `a_%_%`**: Filters values starting with 'a' and having a length of 3 or more.
- **WHERE ContactName LIKE `a%o`**: Matches values starting with 'a' and ending with 'o'.

## Exploiting the % Wildcard

The following SQL snippet selects all customers whose city starts with 'ber':

```sql
SELECT * FROM Customers
WHERE City LIKE 'ber%';

item.title: Tutorial SQL EXISTS Operator
item.description:
SQL EXISTS Operator

The SQL EXISTS operator is utilized to test the existence of records in a subquery.

EXISTS Syntax

SELECT column_name(s)
FROM table_name
WHERE EXISTS
(SELECT column_name FROM table_name WHERE condition);

Demo Database

SQL EXISTS Examples

The following SQL query returns TRUE and lists suppliers with products priced below 20.

SELECT SupplierName
FROM Suppliers
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT ProductName FROM Products WHERE SupplierId = Suppliers.supplierId AND Price < 20);

The next SQL query returns TRUE and lists suppliers with products priced at 22.

item.title: Tutorial SQL IN Operator Explained
item.description:
SQL - IN Operator: Simplifying Multiple Conditions

The SQL IN operator allows the specification of multiple values in the WHERE clause, providing a concise alternative to multiple OR conditions.

IN Syntax

SELECT column_name(s)
FROM table_name
WHERE column_name IN (value1, value2, ...);

or:

SELECT column_name(s)
FROM table_name
WHERE column_name IN (SELECT STATEMENT);

IN Operator Examples

Consider the following SQL query, which selects all customers located in ‘Germany,’ ‘France,’ and ‘UK’:

SELECT * FROM Customers
WHERE Country IN ('Germany', 'France', 'UK');

item.title: Tutorial SQL MIN() and MAX() Functions
item.description:
Exploring SQL MIN() and MAX() Functions

The SQL MIN() and MAX() functions are powerful tools for finding the smallest and largest values in a selected column, respectively.

Understanding MIN() Function

The MIN() function retrieves the smallest value in the specified column.

MIN() Syntax

SELECT MIN(column_name)
FROM table_name
WHERE condition;

MIN() Example

Consider the following SQL query to find the price of the most affordable product:

SELECT MIN(Price) AS SmallestPrice
FROM Products;

This returns the smallest price from the “Products” table.

item.title: Tutorial SQL UNION Operator
item.description:
Learn SQL: Understanding the UNION Operator

SQL UNION operator, a versatile tool for combining result sets from two or more SELECT statements.

Key Features of SQL UNION

  • Each SELECT statement within the UNION must have the same number of columns.
  • Columns should share similar data types.
  • The order of columns in each SELECT statement must align.

SQL UNION Syntax

SELECT column_name(s) FROM table1
UNION
SELECT column_name(s) FROM table2;

item.title: Understanding SQL NULL Values
item.description:
SQL NULL Values

In SQL, NULL represents the absence of a value in a field. When a field in a table is optional, you can insert a new record or update an existing one without providing a value for that field, and the field will be stored as NULL.

Note: It’s essential to understand that a NULL value is different from a field with a value of 0 or an empty string. A field with a NULL value is essentially an empty field created during record creation.

item.title: What is Trigger in SQL? 2023
item.description:
Trigger is a special type of stored procedure that is executed automatically in response to certain events on a database table Triggers are used to enforce business rules, maintain data integrity, and perform tasks such as auditing.

Triggers can be activated by various events, such as INSERT , UPDATE , DELETE , or SELECT statements on a table, or by direct invocation using the EXECUTE or CALL statement. Triggers can also be activated by database events such as logon, logoff, or server startup.

item.description:
A Common Table Expression - CTE in SQL is a named temporary result set that you can reference within a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or CREATE VIEW statement. CTEs are often used to simplify complex queries by breaking them up into smaller, more manageable pieces, or to provide a means of querying hierarchical or recursive data.

CTEs can be used for a variety of purposes, such as:

item.title: What are Triggers in SQL - Amazing knowledge on Triggers 2023
item.description:
SQL triggers are one of the most powerful tools available to database administrators. Triggers in SQL are special type of stored procedure that is executed automatically when certain events occur in a database, such as when data is inserted , updated , or deleted. Triggers can be used to automate a variety of tasks and help streamline the management of databases.

Triggers can be used to enforce data integrity , implement business rules, and enforce security policies. For example, a trigger can be used to ensure that a customer’s address is always stored in the correct format. Triggers can also be used to create audit trails, log changes, and generate notifications. In addition, triggers can be used to update related tables when data in a primary table is modified.
